tables.name: Series
rows: A young witch and her cat Carrot brew potions that rarely go to plan. Pepper&Carrot by David Revoy, www.peppercarrot.com, CC BY 4.0.
Give My Regards to Black Jack
Intern Eijiro Saito earns 38,000 yen a month at a top university hospital and starts asking what it means to be a doctor. Give My Regards to Black Jack, SHUHO SATO.
A high school sysadmin club throws an Ubuntu release party, and a freshman shows up preaching Linux Mint. By Hiroshi Seo; English by Tarek Saier and PublicDesert; CC BY-NC-SA.

tables.name: Chapter
rows: Rule of a Sister Distro! Mint-chan

tables.name: CharacterBio
rows: A young witch who brews potions in a little house on a hill, usually with her cat Carrot as the test subject.
Short on money and with one day to prepare, she hunts wild ingredients to enter Komona's potion challenge.
Pepper's orange cat, who has strong opinions about her potions.
After one sip of the potion of Genius, he starts drawing letters, though maybe not the ones Pepper hopes for.
A wealthy witch from Komona City who buys premium ingredients and loves to tease Pepper.
A market vendor in Komona City who is much friendlier to big spenders.
President of the school's sysadmin club and a devoted Ubunchu (Ubuntu) user.
The club's vice-president, a Windows fan who keeps a 'database' on every girl in school.
A club member and Mac user who mostly enjoys the drama.
A popular student; Akane set up her new Ubunchu install.
A freshman who calls herself Maya Mint, swears by Linux Mint, and has a secret about which distro she really uses.
President of the computer science club, unimpressed by the open-source crowd.
A classmate from Mint's middle school days.
A newly graduated intern at Eiroku University Hospital who takes a part-time night shift at Seido Hospital.
The official addressing Eiroku University's medical graduates at their commencement ceremony.
Saito's exhausted fellow intern at Eiroku University Hospital.
A senior surgeon supervising Saito during an operation at Eiroku University Hospital.
The director of Seido Hospital, who hires Saito for part-time night duty.
The gruff, hard-drinking doctor on night duty at Seido Hospital.
A young man brought in after a motorcycle accident.
Ambulance crew members reporting incoming accident victims, in person and by phone.
The mother of Hiroshi, the young accident victim from the night shift.

tables.name: PageLine
rows: No! Don't even think about it.
A sign on the door: Warning, witch property.
Potion labels: Fire Dance, Deep Ocean, Viole(n)t, Ultra Blue, Meta Pink, Magenta X, Crimson, Nature, Yellow, Orange Top.
Gulp gulp... gulp gulp... gulp gulp
Good morning, sir. I would like eight pumpkinstars, please.
Ko is the Komona currency unit.
Uhh, sorry, I'll have to take only four...
Greetings, good sir. Please prepare two dozen of everything for me. Premium quality, as usual.
It's always a pleasure to serve you, Miss Saffron.
Oh, let me guess, business is booming in the countryside?
I guess you're preparing the ingredients for tomorrow's potion challenge?
Poster: Komona Potion Challenge. 50,000 Ko grand prize for the best potion. On Azarday, 3 Pinkmoon, Grand Plaza of Komona.
Lucky me, I still have a full day to prepare!
Carrot! Get ready, we'll hunt the ingredients together.
First, I need a few pearls of mist from those black clouds...
...and some red berries from the haunted jungle.
...plus egg shells from the Phoenix valley of the volcanos...
...and finally a drop of milk from a young DragonCow.
That's it, Carrot, I think I have everything I need.
Mmm... Best... coffee... ever! It's everything I'll need to work all night long and make the best potion for tomorrow's challenge.
The night before the potion challenge, 2:00 AM.
Finally... With this potion, no one, not even Saffron, can match my skill! I do need to test it on someone...
Amazing! Not even under the bed?
I really didn't think I would have to use this trick...
Awww, Carrot! You sweet kitty cat, you've come all by yourself! At the very moment when I need my favorite assistant.
Here, I present you my final masterpiece: the potion of Genius.
If it works, you should have a stroke of genius!
Wow... Carrot! That's amazing... A real alphabet...
C'mon Carrot, I'm running out of words. This really doesn't make any sense!
Grrrrrrr!!! Nothing ever works with me!
Bah... I still have time to invent another potion.
Chapter 12: Rule of a sister distro! Mint-chan.
A scene we're all too familiar with?!
A release party. A sacred celebration for us Ubunteros to mark a new version release. But...
Behold the sight of all those who care. But a single fanatic geek.
I was sure people were coming...!
Worry not! It's not too late to change.
Windows 8 is soon to be released. I'm sure you'll like it.
We'll go to the midnight release at Akiba!
This is how I imagined it to be. Which of course... of course...
To be real, though, half of the people are just here for Urara.
Let me dream just one more minute.
Alright, that's my chance to give a great speech!
She's so not good with situations like this...
Hah... hasn't tingled for a while...
That girl... is she a student here?
Not sure if I've seen her before...
Such a beauty. No way she wouldn't be in my database...
And that's... uh... that sums up the new features in Ubunchu!
The end. Thank you for your attention.
For the remaining time, let's chat and have tea.
A bit sudden, I guess, but... would it be okay to do a lightning talk?
A lightning talk is a short presentation, about five minutes, usually done at technical conferences.
It's actually just a nickname. Feel free to call me "Mint".
So she's using... Linux Mint! Maya is the current version's codename.
It's not Ubunchu? But it's Linux...
Erm... there are actually a lot of operating systems that are Linux...
Imagine the Linux kernel in the center, with all the software for users around it.
We call that a distribution, or "distro" for short.
There's a plethora of distros, all differing in software and settings.
And Ubunchu is just one of them.
Linux Mint is based on Ubunchu, so it's like a child of Ubunchu.
Ubunchu itself, by the way, is the child of a distro called Debian.
I see! Mint is the loved daughter of our Ubunchu.
As you can clearly see on this popularity ranking, Mint is the number one!
Ubunchu is a thing of the past. Linux Mint is where it's at!
Let's see... Urara, I bet your fresh Ubunchu install wouldn't play DVDs, right?
True. Akane was kind enough to help me with that.
Not that I could follow what she did. But it works now.
See? That's the issue. Repository? Command? Device?
You can't expect the average user to know how to do things like adding repositories.
With Mint, codecs are included from the start. Media just plays on a fresh install.
That's the first reason for Mint's popularity.
Did... did any of you maybe struggle getting used to Unity?
A sudden change of how everything looks is totally off-putting.
Mint comes with a look that most people are used to already.
The second reason for Mint's popularity.
Last but not least... since Mint is an Ubunchu derivative, they have a lot in common!
The third reason for Mint's popularity: it's easy for Ubunchu users to make the switch.
Here... I brought some installation DVDs.
Ubunchu not coming with codecs is due to licensing problems.
And Japanese support in Mint is still kind of buggy. I wouldn't...
Not that I have anything against Mint... but does she really have to be so pushy?
Hold on! LMDE? But that is not at all...
LMDE, which is not a derivative of Ubunchu but of Debian.
Which means this doesn't have all that much in common with Ubunchu, making it actually not that easy to switch over to.
Err... oh well, I don't really follow. That's too technical for me.
Maya Mint, your real name is...
Translator's note: uzumaki means spiral or swirl in Japanese. In the original, Maki Uzui's nickname is Uzumaki.
I'm the girl that's been using Debian since junior high.
I was proud of using Debian. No frills, pure efficiency.
In high school, I made sure no one would find out. But...
Some dimwit started picking on me.
Spiral Eyes uses a spiral OS!
I got more and more frustrated, and thought...
Ubunchu is just a Debian derivative.
If I changed my image by using a more popular distro, maybe even someone like me would...
I have never met a girl that uses Debian!
Ubunchu exists because of Debian! We have so much to...
I... I'm not swayed that easily...
Did you by any chance not hear the bell ring!? School's over.
Go ahead. Cat fight for that 1% user share. Be careful not to make the boys too excited.
We're not really going to fight, right? Right...?
The speaker pauses on the figure of 8000.
He states that 8000 students graduate each year from the country's 81 medical universities.
He tells the assembled graduates that they are the top eighty of those 8000.
He proclaims that the future of Japanese medicine is in their hands.
A colleague remarks that Saito looks sleepy.
Saito explains he has just come off a shift.
Saito says he has been at the hospital for more than 24 hours, since the previous morning.
His colleague says the same goes for him.
He explains he was assisting with a doctor's experiments.
He complains that he got only three hours of sleep.
Saito grins that he slept just two hours.
Saito reflects that three months have passed since he graduated from Eiroku University.
He notes that he now works as an intern at the university's hospital.
A senior surgeon prods Saito to get on with it.
He scolds Saito for grimacing every time he gives an injection.
Saito explains that interns are essentially apprentices.
He notes that becoming a doctor means six years at a medical university...
...followed by passing the national medical licensing examination.
He points out that the licensing exam tests only medical knowledge.
He stresses that there is no practical exam.
That, he explains, is why most graduates spend two years as interns at a university hospital.
The surgeon tells Saito to widen the incision.
He says he hates himself for being able to enjoy a meal right after an operation.
He starts to confide something to Saito.
He worries that the job is wearing away his ability to care about others.
Saito asks what he is talking about.
Saito insists that they are the ones holding up Japan's medical care.
Saito notes that interns work about 16 hours a day on average.
He builds up to the amount of his monthly salary...
He clarifies that this is his monthly pay, not his daily pay.
He adds that his hospital is not unusually stingy; public hospitals...
...pay slightly more, yet about 70% of interns at private university hospitals earn under $1200 a month.
He observes that nobody could cover food and rent on such a salary.
He tells Saito that his part-time shift at this hospital begins today.
He reads out Saito's profile: Eijiro Saito, 25 years old.
He notes that Saito graduated from Eiroku University's medical department.
He observes that this is Saito's first time on duty.
He remarks on Saito being from Eiroku.
He comments that Saito must be one of the elite.
He vows not to tarnish Eiroku's good name.
The director mentions that another doctor is also on duty since it is Saito's first day.
He tells Saito to ask that doctor how things work.
Saito reflects that this is what intern life really looks like.
Saito greets the doctor on duty.
He introduces himself as a part-time doctor from Eiroku.
He introduces himself again and says he is here for the shift.
Ushida advises him to eat whenever he gets the chance.
He adds sleeping to the list.
He advises Saito to sleep whenever he gets the chance.
Saito reads the hospital's name from its records.
He notes that it has 120 beds.
He muses that it is a fairly large hospital serving most of the local residents.
He notes that there are only three doctors.
He works out that the first man he met was the director and the other was Mr. Ushida.
He realizes that tonight it is only him and Mr. Ushida.
The injured man begs for help.
Ushida urges Saito to hurry, warning that it is about to become a war zone.
A paramedic reports a 20-year-old man who came off his motorcycle about 30 minutes ago.
He adds that the man's left leg is shattered.
Ushida orders a blood count, blood typing and a full chemistry panel, stat.
He calls out to Saito as the Eiroku grad.
He orders a Lactec injection and a dose of hydrocodone.
He yells at Saito to hurry.
He tells Saito to cross-match the patient's blood when he is done.
He admits he was no help at all.
Ushida tells him he has no time to feel down.
He reports that the woman's blood pressure is falling.
Ushida tells him to be quiet and give her the transfusion.
He says that anyone who can scream that much will be fine.
Over the phone, a paramedic reports an accident victim.
He reports an irregular heartbeat and difficulty breathing.
The next call reports a man in his sixties.
He is still unconscious after a head-on collision at a traffic light.
Saito marvels at how capable Mr. Ushida is.
Ushida asks Saito, whom he calls Eiroku, what he is smiling about.
Saito says this hospital is amazing.
He admires how it never turns away an ambulance.
Ushida tells him to stop sounding like an amateur.
He explains that everything a doctor does is billed on a point system...
...giving examples of how many points an enema or a blood draw is worth.
He explains that the doctor is paid the point total out of health insurance.
Diagram: a sample bill (first visit, night visit, ultrasound and blood tests) totaling 1,433 points, or $169.88.
He adds that every point is worth 10 cents across the board.
Ushida says traffic accidents work differently.
He explains that the bill is covered by vehicle liability insurance rather than health insurance.
He notes that the price is therefore up to the doctor's discretion.
He explains that in such cases a doctor can set the value of a point himself.
Saito starts to piece it together.
He asks whether a doctor can charge whatever he likes for a traffic accident patient.
Ushida asks whether he really hadn't noticed.
He reveals that the hospital only takes traffic accident patients.
Ushida says this hospital charges 40 cents a point for traffic accidents.
He admits that is four times the normal rate.
He says that in the end it is all about money.
He adds that they are not doing this out of public service.
Saito notes that he earned 948 dollars.
He realizes he made more than twice his monthly intern salary in a single night.
His colleague says he again slept only three hours.
He grumbles that interns must be the unhealthiest people on earth.
He asks how the part-time job went.
Saito asks who the covered patient is.
His colleague says it looks like another patient has died.
Saito brings up the $948 he was paid...
...and asks whether it is really all right to take it.
His colleague asks why it wouldn't be.
He points out that Saito worked hard for it.
He trails off, troubled by this kind of money.
Saito says he does not want to become a corrupt doctor.
His colleague starts to confess something.
He admits he never really wanted to be a doctor.
He says he just rode the exam-war escalator, pushing to reach the top...
...and suddenly found that he had become a doctor.
He repeats the word 'doctor' to himself.
He wonders what that even means.
The director offers Saito $1186 for tonight.
He says Saito will be on his own from tonight on.
He offers to pay more if that isn't enough.
He tries to say that isn't what he meant.
The director asks if he is nervous about working alone.
The director states that there are currently 240,000 doctors in Japan.
He asks what that number tells Saito.
Saito answers that it means about one doctor for every 500 people.
He says no other developed country can beat that.
He says Saito is forgetting something important.
He names the missing factor: the number of hospitals.
He explains that Japan has many doctors but an absurd number of hospitals.
He says that is why even a hospital this size has only three doctors.
...Japan has extremely few doctors per hospital.
Saito says he already knows that.
He reminds Saito that doctors are people with families too.
He says three doctors could never cover day and night shifts every day.
Saito feels he has just done something very wrong.
Saito admits he needed the money to live.
He notes that at night, a hospital often has only interns on duty.
He adds that outside university hospitals this is not unusual...
...in fact, for Japanese hospitals it is simply common sense.
He warns that if you don't want to die, you shouldn't drive at night.
He says that if you do get into an accident, the chance of being treated by an experienced doctor is...
Caption: this is what night looks like in Japan.
A survey of 79 university hospitals nationwide found that no more than 2% prohibited their interns from part-time work.
80% of the interns doing part-time work had treated patients without supervision.
Furthermore, over 90% of the interns treating patients unsupervised did so while feeling uneasy.
Source: a survey by the Association of Independent Japanese Medical Students.
A paramedic reports a traffic accident: male, mid-20s.
He lists trauma, bruising and likely multiple fractures throughout the body.
He gives a consciousness level of 30.
A paramedic calls to get the man to a hospital immediately.
Another answers that they are ready to go.
A nurse confirms they are ready to accept the patient.
She announces that the ambulance will arrive in 10 minutes.
A nurse urges the doctor to hurry to the operating room.
Saito snaps that he heard her.
Saito nervously says hello into the phone.
He starts asking for Mr. Ushida.
Ushida's cheerful answering-machine greeting cuts him off.
Saito yells for Mr. Ushida to wake up.
He shouts that it is an emergency.
He warns that they may need to operate.
A nurse calls for the doctor.
She announces that the ambulance has arrived.
Saito realizes that the man's internal organs have ruptured.
The director's answering machine says he can't come to the phone.
It asks the caller to leave a message after the beep.
A nurse anxiously asks the doctor what is happening.
A nurse says he isn't coming back.
Saito curses that the director isn't home either.
Saito whispers that he can't do it.
Saito says the liver is ruptured and there is a perforation somewhere in the digestive tract.
He stammers that he has never performed an operation this major.
He asks himself what he is going to do.
He says the patient is going to die.
He repeats that he just can't do it.
A nurse addresses the director in surprise.
The director says the head nurse called him.
He addresses him as Dr. Saito.
He asks how the patient is.
The director asks why Saito didn't operate.
He says the patient would die if left alone.
He argues that if the man was going to die anyway, Saito might as well have opened him up...
He says that if he made a mistake, he would be a murderer.
The director says trying is better than doing nothing.
He accuses Saito of being ready to let the patient die without even trying.
He blames the hospital for leaving an intern alone all night.
He says a hospital without enough doctors shouldn't accept patients.
He accuses the director of caring only about money.
The director coolly asks, so what?
He says they are saving lives.
He asks what is wrong with overcharging for that.
He asks what his taking people's money...
...has to do with Saito refusing to operate.
He reminds Saito that he is a doctor...
...and that however new or inexperienced he is, to the patient he is still a doctor.
He asks if Saito really thinks botching an operation makes him a murderer.
He says that, in the end, the patient is to blame for causing the accident.
He orders Saito to operate no matter what.
He tells him to drop the lofty philosophical arguments.
He says being right only means being weak.
He says Saito stopped being an ordinary person the moment he got his medical license.
He tells him that he is a doctor.
He tells Saito to be strong.
He admits he was too drunk to notice the phone call.
He asks if Saito is feeling down again.
Ushida says that a long time ago...
...he also objected to what the director was doing.
He recalls telling the director that his methods were wrong.
And that a hospital is not a tool for making money.
He says that is what he told him.
He says he still thinks the director is wrong.
He says that satisfying yourself with being right changes nothing.
He admits that the truth is...
...that the director is saving people's lives.
A woman cries out in relief that he is okay.
She calls Hiroshi by name, overjoyed that he is really okay.
Saito wonders what it really means to be a doctor.

tables.name: Comment
rows: Carrot's face on the last page is everything.
Best cat in comics, no contest.
Masato's 'database' is the most cursed app in this club.
FREE manga downloads at my site, click my profile!!!
Agreed. That look says 'I knew it'.

rows: Too graphic for a general audience
